title: August minutes weigh an insurance hike against early evidence that housing and demand are cooling
summary: The 10–11 August meeting ended in a unanimous hold at 4.35%. In minutes published on 25 August, the Board recorded an explicit alternative of a 25 basis point increase. Some members thought there was a meaningful chance that upside risks would soon require further tightening. Others saw downside risks partly offsetting them. What united the nine was the value of the information due before their next meeting. Several indicators were moving towards the inflation and employment objectives, and financial conditions looked restrictive enough to permit waiting. The vote established agreement about timing without resolving the disagreement about the probability of the next move (Considerations for monetary policy and The decision).

Inflation remained materially above target despite a weaker headline result than forecast. Retail fuel and travel prices contributed most to the undershoot. Trimmed mean inflation reached 3.6% in the June quarter on the year-ended measure and fell only slightly short of staff expectations. Members associated elevated market-services inflation with domestic capacity constraints. New-dwelling prices showed pass-through of higher construction inputs, while transmission into other consumer prices appeared somewhat smaller than anticipated in May. The unresolved issue was whether firms were delaying increases or accepting a permanent compression in margins because customers were price-sensitive. Future movements in petrol alone could not distinguish those outcomes (Economic conditions).

The underlying oil path was broadly in line with May’s forecast despite successive reversals in the conflict. The quantity of oil and refined products held in global inventories, however, had fallen. A future disruption starting with smaller buffers could have a different effect even if the spot price on the meeting date matched the previous forecast. At the same time, AI-related demand had repeatedly boosted growth in East Asian trading partners beyond expectations. It could raise Australian import costs where supply of components was constrained. Technology-sector funding was also becoming more selective, with some bond spreads widening and highly leveraged equity positions being unwound. The direct expenditure caused by data-centre construction and the eventual return to its financiers were separate variables (Financial conditions and Economic conditions).

The domestic slowdown was visible first in established housing. National house prices had fallen about 1½% from March, more than expected in May, but remained roughly 5% higher than a year earlier and 50% higher than at the onset of the pandemic. New loan demand had declined sharply, especially among investors. Earlier increases in the cash rate, announced tax changes and weaker sentiment could all have contributed. Scheduled mortgage payments as a share of disposable income were approaching the 2024 peak. Additional repayments had fallen but remained near their long-run average. Many existing borrowers had buffers. Falling prices and weaker new borrowing therefore did not imply an immediate, equivalent fall in aggregate consumption (Financial conditions and Economic conditions).

Household spending momentum was slowing only gradually despite very weak consumer confidence. Private investment had grown strongly in the March quarter, particularly in data-centre fit-outs, and business debt growth remained broad. The labour market had eased slightly more than anticipated but leading indicators pointed to limited further easing in the near term. Firms continued to report difficulties obtaining suitable workers and cost pressure across inputs. Staff lowered the forecast level of productivity following earlier weak outcomes while retaining the medium-term assumption for its growth rate. If yesterday’s output per hour turns out to have been lower, tomorrow’s level of potential output can be lower even while projected subsequent growth rates are unchanged (Economic conditions and Economic outlook).

The central projection had GDP growing below potential, with demand and productive capacity broadly balanced in 2027. Unemployment was projected to reach 4.8% by end-2028. Labour-market spare capacity would start to emerge in late 2027, gradually restraining wages despite the near-term effect of recent awards and agreements. Trimmed mean inflation remained over 3% until mid-2027 and returned to around 2.5% in late 2027. Its interest-rate assumption came from the market curve, which ended the forecast period near the prevailing rate. That conditional profile gave the hold camp a coherent path to the objective while leaving output, oil, pricing and productivity risks on both sides (Economic outlook and Considerations for monetary policy).

External demand also depended on which parts of Asia were buying. In China, weak household spending and property investment weighed on private demand and steel consumption. Infrastructure spending and exports provided offsets, while official support concentrated on manufacturing, robotics, AI and green technology. Strong aggregate growth in Australia’s trading partners could therefore coexist with quite different prospects for an exporter exposed to Chinese housing and one supplying technology investment elsewhere in the region (Financial conditions and Economic outlook).

The strongest case for an increase paired upside risks with two findings from staff research. When spare capacity is limited, a small change in capacity use can be associated with a comparatively large change in inflation. Short-term expectations can also influence price-setting even when longer-term beliefs appear anchored. If those relationships held in the present episode, a precautionary increase could lower inflation with a smaller employment cost than in some past cycles. Risks included depleted oil stocks, broader transmission of costs, stronger data-centre demand and weaker productivity. Conversely, softer hiring, a deeper housing downturn or customers resisting price rises could bring inflation down sooner. Members did not treat the research relationships as stable policy multipliers (Considerations for monetary policy).

Markets saw little chance of an August increase and roughly an even chance of another quarter-point increase by year-end. Most surveyed economists expected no further hike and some anticipated easing in early 2027. Long real bond yields were near their highest levels in more than 15 years, while high short-run inflation expectations left shorter real yields much lower. The trade-weighted Australian dollar had fallen about 1% since May but was up about 5% year-to-date. Attributing any of these multi-month changes to an anticipated August hold would confuse a policy setting with its surprise. New monthly inflation and employment data plus the June-quarter national accounts would shortly allow a better assessment. Separately, the Board backed leaving APRA’s prudential settings unchanged and judged financial stability posed no immediate constraint on the cash-rate decision (Financial conditions, Considerations for monetary policy and Financial stability advice).

questions.question: Was disappointing productivity supply-related, or a temporary result of how output and labour are measured?
questions.detail: Rebuild the staff’s productivity history using data vintages available in August. Separate changes in measured hours, sector composition and investment under construction. Compare industries with recruitment difficulty against those with weaker sales. A persistent downward level revision has different implications for capacity from a temporary surge in hours before a long-lived project begins producing services.

questions.question: Did housing weakness transmit into consumption through wealth, or through borrowing and transactions?
questions.detail: Compare investor and owner-occupier lending, turnover, prices and purchases related to moving home around tax and rate changes. Adjust for prior price gains and the local share of highly indebted homeowners. Similar price declines can produce different spending responses depending on mortgage buffers and refinancing exposure. Reduced transactions can affect activity even when existing owners make little wealth-related spending adjustment.

questions.question: How does the price response to a supply shock change when inventories are already depleted?
questions.detail: Match unexpected disruptions to crude and refined product prices while conditioning on stocks, refining capacity and demand. Track Australian input prices, selling-price plans and realised inflation separately. Test whether otherwise comparable shocks generate larger and more persistent price effects after inventory drawdowns. Treat the August futures path as an assumption available then, preserving later forecasts as separate vintages.
